title: You Are That Man: Nathan Confronts David
summary: The LORD sends Nathan the prophet to David with a parable about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb. When David condemns the rich man, Nathan tells him, “You are that man,” and announces God's judgment: the sword will never depart from his house. David confesses, Nathan declares his sin taken away, but the child born to Bathsheba dies; afterward Solomon is born and loved by the LORD, and the Ammonite capital Rabbah is finally captured.
story: Chapter 11 ended with the narrator's quiet verdict that David's deed was evil in the sight of the LORD. Chapter 12 shows God acting on that verdict. The king who could not be judged by any human court is judged by the word of God, spoken through a prophet. The chapter holds together two things that run through the rest of 2 Samuel: forgiveness and consequences. David is forgiven and does not die, but Nathan's words in verses 10-12 become the outline of the chapters to come, as sexual violence, murder, and rebellion break out within David's own family (chapters 13-18). Solomon, born at the end of the chapter, is the son through whom the promise of chapter 7 will continue.
historical:
Prophets in Israel had a remarkable role: they could confront kings in God's name. Samuel had rebuked Saul (1 Samuel 13 and 15), and later Elijah would confront Ahab, whose theft of Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21) is a close cousin of this story. Other ancient Near Eastern courts had prophets, as texts from the city of Mari on the Euphrates show, but they rarely condemned their king so directly for a moral crime against one of his subjects.

The siege of Rabbah, begun in chapter 11, ends here, though the account in verses 26-31 is placed after the birth of Solomon and probably took place well before it, since a long siege would not have outlasted two pregnancies. Joab captures the royal fortress and the city's water supply, and then calls David to take the city so that the king, not the general, receives the credit. The crown in verse 30 weighed a talent, roughly thirty kilograms or more, which suggests it may have belonged to a statue. The Hebrew word for their king (malkam) is very close to Milcom, the name of the Ammonite god, and the Greek translation and several modern versions read it that way.
cultural:
Nathan's parable works because it appeals to David as a judge. The king was Israel's final court of appeal, and a poor man wronged by a powerful neighbor was exactly the kind of case he was meant to hear. Hospitality required a host to feed a traveler, which is why the rich man needed an animal, and the detail that the lamb “was like a daughter to him” makes the theft unbearable. David's sentence mixes outrage with law: the Torah required fourfold restitution for a stolen and slaughtered sheep (Exodus 22:1).

David's mourning customs also stand out. Fasting, lying on the ground, and wearing sackcloth (coarse cloth of goat hair) were signs of grief and of pleading with God. Normally these were done after a death, not before it; David reverses the expected order, pleading while the child lives and then washing, worshiping, and eating once he has died. His servants are bewildered, and his explanation is one of the most quoted passages in the chapter. Verse 31 has been read in two ways: older translations took it as the torture of prisoners with saws and brick kilns, while most modern translations, including the BSB, understand it as forced labor.
literary: The chapter hinges on Nathan's parable (verses 1-4), a trap in the form of a legal case. David hears a story about someone else and pronounces judgment, then discovers that he has sentenced himself. The four words “You are that man” are the turning point of David's whole story. God's speech that follows (verses 7-12) rehearses God's generosity (I anointed, I delivered, I gave, and I would have given more) before naming the sin, and its punishments mirror the crime: David used the sword, so the sword will not leave his house; he took another man's wife in secret, so his wives will be taken in broad daylight. David's confession is two words in Hebrew, and Nathan's pardon is almost as brief.

outline.t: Nathan's parable of the rich man and the poor man's lamb
You are that man: the LORD's judgment
Solomon is born, and the LORD names him Jedidiah

doctrines.note: David's response, “I have sinned against the LORD,” is plain and unguarded: no excuses, no blaming Bathsheba or Joab. Unlike Saul, who made excuses when confronted (1 Samuel 15), David owns his sin before God. Psalm 51, which its heading ties to this moment, gives the longer prayer.

Forgiveness does not erase every consequence. God takes away the guilt that would have cost David his life, yet the child dies and the sword remains in his house. The chapter refuses both cheap grace and endless condemnation.
God speaks through a prophet to a king. The word of the LORD stands above the throne, and even Israel's greatest king must hear it and submit.
David pleads for the child's life on the chance that “The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live,” and when God says no, he worships. Prayer here is both bold asking and humble acceptance.

words.note: Chata, to sin. The basic idea is to miss a mark or fall short of what is required. David's confession uses it in the simplest form possible: I have sinned against the LORD. Though David wronged Bathsheba and Uriah, he names God as the one sinned against, as Psalm 51:4 also does, because every wrong against a person made in God's image is finally a wrong against him.
Avar, to pass over or cause to pass away. Nathan says the LORD has made David's sin pass away, which the BSB renders taken away. The picture is of guilt carried off, removed from the one who bore it.

Naats, to spurn or treat with contempt. It appears twice in verse 14, which the BSB renders shown utter contempt. Sin here is not only a broken rule but an insult to the God who had given David everything.
Chanan, to be gracious, to show favor that is not earned. David fasts because the LORD “may be gracious” (verse 22). His hope rests not on a right to the child's life but on God's freedom to give.

christ: David is forgiven, yet someone still dies, and the chapter leaves the reader with the question of how a just God can take away sin. The New Testament answers that God takes away sin at his own cost in the death of Christ, the son of David, who bore what sinners deserved (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). The child's death is not a picture of the atonement and should not be pressed into one; it is part of David's discipline. But the chapter's pairing of real guilt, real confession, and real forgiveness from God prepares for the gospel. Paul quotes the psalm of David on the blessing of the one whose sin is forgiven (Romans 4:6-8, from Psalm 32), and the name Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD, finds a thematic echo (not a prediction) in the Father's word over Jesus at his baptism, “This is My beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17).

hard.q: Why should an innocent child die for his father's sin?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest lines in Samuel, and the text does not soften it. Several things can be said without explaining it away. The law of Moses forbade human courts from executing children for their fathers' crimes (Deuteronomy 24:16), so the text is not describing human justice but God's sovereign act as the giver and taker of life. The Old Testament often shows the sins of leaders falling on their households, a reality of human life as much as a divine sentence. Some interpreters read the death as sparing the child a life marked as the product of adultery and murder; others think that is speculation. David's words in verse 23, “I will go to him, but he will not return to me,” have been read as hope of reunion after death, and many Christians have drawn comfort from them regarding children who die young; others take them to mean only that David too will go to the grave. What the chapter does not do is present the child's death as good. It shows David grieving, pleading, and finally worshiping a God he cannot fully understand.

questions: David could see the rich man's sin clearly but not his own. Why is it easier to judge others than ourselves?
David was forgiven but still faced consequences. How do you understand the relationship between forgiveness and consequences?
After the child died, David worshiped. What does his response teach about grief and trust when prayer is not answered as we hoped?
